title: BTP structure: accounts, directories, subaccounts
summary: How a BTP landscape is organized: global account → directories → subaccounts → services & environments.
explain:
BTP structure is hierarchical so companies can separate billing, teams, and stages.

1) Global account — commercial root (contracts, overall entitlements).
2) Directories — optional folders for org units or regions.
3) Subaccounts — isolation units where you enable services, assign members, create destinations, and deploy apps.
4) Environments — e.g. Cloud Foundry / Kyma / ABAP environment inside a subaccount.
5) Entitlements & service plans — what you are allowed to run and at which tier.

Rule of thumb: Dev / Test / Prod as separate subaccounts (or cleanly separated spaces with strong process) to avoid ‘works on my subaccount’ disasters.

Fidelity: conceptual — UI labels evolve; verify in your cockpit.
analogy: Global account = company HQ. Directories = floors. Subaccounts = locked rooms for projects. Environments = workbenches inside a room. Entitlements = keys HQ issued for tools.
whyItMatters: Most beginner confusion is not CAP vs RAP — it is ‘where do I create this service and who can see it?’ Wrong structure causes security and cost leaks.
formalPoints: Global account is the commercial root
Subaccounts isolate apps, members, destinations, and service instances
Entitlements gate which services/plans exist where
commonMistakes: One shared subaccount for everything ‘to go faster’
Granting admin to everyone at global account for convenience
Forgetting destinations and identity are per-subaccount concerns
howToRecognize: Setup conversations, landing zone design, first service enablement
howToApply: Draw your landing zone: global → directories → dev/test/prod subaccounts
List who is admin at each level
